newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn must do more than revalue gold-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bonn must do more than revalue gold-analysts.

text.p: A plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves has sparked a whirl of controversy, but the Finance Ministry will have to do more to get Germany's budget deficit in line, analysts said on Friday.

While the ministry has proposed adjusting the book value of the central bank's foreign currency reserves as well as its gold, it is also considering freezing spending, raising taxes and selling real estate and shares in state-owned enterprises sooner than expected.
"The problem is solvable, but there is no simple recipe," Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), said in a television interview.

Revaluing the Bundesbank's 95 million ounces of gold could put 40 billion more marks into Bonn's book, helping to reduce its old debt. But it will have to resort to other measures to bring down its 1997 deficit, a task made harder on Thursday by news of an expected 18 billion mark shortfall in tax revenues.

"Waigel said the money would not be used for the deficit, only debt," said Norbert Braems, chief economist at private bank Sal. Oppenheim in Cologne. To cut the deficit, "they will definitely cut spending any way they can."
The gold is now held on the Bundesbank's books at 144 marks an ounce, even though the current market price is about 660 marks per ounce.
Oppposition Social Democrats (SPD) and tabloid newspapers have denounced the proposal as "budget trickery," but other European Union nations regularly revalue their reserves.
Bonn could also revalue the Bundesbank's reserves of dollars and other foreign currencies, Waigel announced on Thursday.
The dollar's rise to 1.70 marks has increased the value of much of the foreign currency the central bank holds in reserve.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats, firmly opposed to tax increases, backed the idea of revaluing assets to free funds to pay off debts.

But Glos said increased taxes were another possible measure. The coalition and SPD have already discussed possible increases in value-added tax and petrol tax as part of a massive tax reform proposal.

But the FDP has taken a hard line against any hikes. "They are out of the question," FDP finance chief Carl-Ludwig Thiele told Saarlaendischer Rundfunk on Friday. Tax hikes would be "poison to the economy," he added.
Waigel and the FDP both support the idea of selling Bonn's shares in companies such as phone company Deutsche Telekom AG and Postbank AG, the former banking arm of the German post office.

Bonn could also sell its 26 percent share of the Frankfurt airport and shares in more than 400 other companies and real estate holdings, the FDP's Rainer Bruederle told the Allgemeinen Zeitung in Mainz.
"The state should systematically pull out of these stakes," he said. German states and communities could also divest holding in another 1,000 companies, the Federation of German Industry (BDI) said.

Bonn is also counting on lower transfers to the EU. The tax estimate released on Thursday said Bonn now expected to transer 42.1 billion marks to the EU this year, down 200 million marks from its November estimate.
